summary: The original Path Computation Element protocol let a PCE compute paths but did not let it track the state of existing label switched paths. This document adds extensions so a stateful PCE can synchronize LSP state with clients and, where allowed, take control of path parameters.

plainLanguage.summary: Stateful PCEP lets a path computation server track the routes that are already in use and, with permission, change some of them. The router still owns its routes and can take back control at any time.

how does delegation work in pcep
subtitle: How a path computation server can learn about, and take control of, label switched paths it computes paths for.

tldr.problem: The original PCEP let a Path Computation Element (PCE) compute paths, but it gave the PCE no view of existing LSPs and no way to control when path computations take effect.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 8231 adds capability advertisement, state synchronization, LSP state reports (PCRpt), update requests (PCUpd), and per-LSP delegation so a PCE can learn LSP state and, when delegated, update LSPs.
tldr.outcome: A PCE can keep an up-to-date view of a PCC's LSPs and, for delegated LSPs, decide when and how to change them. The PCC retains ownership of LSP state. It is updated by later RFCs.

today: RFC 8231 is a Proposed Standard. It has not been obsoleted, but it is updated by RFC 8786, RFC 9353, RFC 9753, RFC 9756 and RFC 9862.

sections.title: Why a Stateful PCE
sections.content:
The original Path Computation Element Communication Protocol (PCEP) defined in RFC 5440 allows a Path Computation Client (PCC) to ask a Path Computation Element (PCE) to compute paths for MPLS Traffic Engineering Label Switched Paths (LSPs). It provides no way for the PCE to see existing LSPs or to control the timing and sequence of changes.

RFC 8231 addresses this for MPLS-TE and GMPLS LSPs. A PCE that sees global LSP state can make better decisions for some traffic engineering problems. The extensions support both passive operation (reporting only) and active operation (updating LSPs when delegated), with the PCC retaining state ownership.
sections.plainLanguage: A planner that only answers when asked does not know what routes are already in use. If the planner is told about all routes, it can plan better. The owner of the routes can still say yes or no to changes.

sections.title: Active, Passive and Delegation
sections.content:
A Passive Stateful PCE receives LSP State Reports from a PCC so it can maintain an up-to-date view of the PCC's LSPs. An Active Stateful PCE can also update LSP attributes for LSPs that have been delegated to it.

State ownership remains with the PCC. The PCC may delegate specific LSPs to a PCE at any time, and it may revoke that delegation at any time. The PCE may return delegation. Only one PCE controls a given LSP at a time. A PCC can talk to stateless and stateful PCEs at once.
sections.plainLanguage: A passive helper only watches and takes notes. An active helper may be given the steering wheel for a particular route, but the owner of that route can take the wheel back whenever they want.

sections.title: Capability Advertisement
sections.content:
During PCEP session setup, each speaker advertises the optional STATEFUL-PCE-CAPABILITY TLV in its OPEN object (Type 16, Length 4). The only defined flag is the U flag (LSP-UPDATE-CAPABILITY). A passive stateful speaker sets U to 0; an active stateful speaker sets U to 1.

The stateful extensions MUST NOT be used unless both speakers include the TLV. LSP delegation and LSP updates require U to be set to 1 on both sides. Even if U is not set, a PCE can act as a passive stateful PCE and accept LSP State Reports.
sections.plainLanguage: Before working together, both sides say what they can do. Only if both agree to allow changes can the helper actually change routes.

sections.title: State Synchronization
sections.content:
Immediately after session initialization, the PCC sends the PCE a snapshot of its LSP state as a sequence of LSP State Reports in PCRpt messages, with the SYNC flag set to 1 for each. Synchronization ends when the PCC sends a PCRpt with SYNC set to 0 for an LSP object with PLSP-ID 0.

While synchronization is in progress, the PCE SHOULD NOT send PCUpd messages, and the PCC SHOULD NOT send PCReq messages. If the PCE encounters an error during synchronization, it MUST send a PCErr with Error-type 20 (LSP State Synchronization Error) and terminate the session. If the PCC cannot complete synchronization, it MUST send Error-type 20 with error-value 5 and terminate the session.
sections.plainLanguage: When the helper first connects, the router gives it a complete list of all routes it is currently using. A final message marks the list as complete.

sections.title: Delegation, Revocation and Return
sections.content:
The PCC grants delegation by setting the D (Delegate) flag to 1 in a PCRpt. It must keep D set to 1 on every report for that delegation to continue. A PCE that accepts delegation replies with an empty PCUpd with D set to 1; a PCE that does not accept replies with D set to 0.

The PCC can revoke delegation at any time by sending a PCRpt with D set to 0 (ideally reverting to operator parameters in a make-before-break fashion). The PCE can return delegation by sending a PCUpd with D set to 0. If a PCE sends a PCUpd for an LSP that is not delegated, the PCC MUST respond with a PCErr (Error-type 19, error-value 1).

Two timers handle PCE failure: the Redelegation Timeout Interval (how long the PCC waits after unexpected session loss before revoking delegations and trying another PCE), and the State Timeout Interval (how long it waits before flushing PCE-set state and reverting to operator defaults). The State Timeout MUST be at least the Redelegation Timeout.
sections.plainLanguage: The router can lend the steering wheel for a specific route. Either side can take it back. If the helper disappears unexpectedly, the router waits a little while and then either finds another helper or goes back to its original plan.

sections.title: PCRpt and PCUpd Messages
sections.content:
The PCRpt message (Message-Type 10) reports the state of one or more LSPs from the PCC to the PCE, either asynchronously or in response to an update. Each PCRpt must include the LSP object and the intended path (ERO). The PCUpd message (Message-Type 11) is sent by the PCE to request changes; each update must include the SRP object, the LSP object, and an ERO.

The PCC MUST respond to every processed PCUpd with a PCRpt that includes the SRP-ID-number from the update. When making changes, the PCC SHOULD minimize traffic loss and may use make-before-break procedures (RFC 3209). If updates arrive faster than the PCC can process them, the PCC may compress its queue and process only the latest update for a given LSP.
sections.plainLanguage: The router sends reports about route states. The helper sends requests to change routes. Every change request gets an answer, and the answer includes a reference number so they can be matched.

sections.title: SRP and LSP Objects
sections.content:
The SRP object (Class 33, Type 1) correlates PCUpd requests with the PCRpt responses. Its SRP-ID-number is a 32-bit value that is incremented per request; values 0x00000000 and 0xFFFFFFFF are reserved. An SRP-ID-number of 0 is used when a PCRpt is not triggered by a PCUpd.

The LSP object (Class 32, Type 1) identifies the target LSP and carries flags including D (delegate), S (sync), R (remove), and A (administrative), plus a 3-bit operational state (O). The PLSP-ID is 20 bits and remains constant for the session (0 and 0xFFFFF reserved).

Key TLVs include SYMBOLIC-PATH-NAME (Type 17), which provides a stable name unique to the PCC across restarts and sessions, LSP-IDENTIFIERS TLVs (IPv4/IPv6), and error TLVs used to report failures.
sections.plainLanguage: Each change request gets a ticket number. Each route gets a short ID and a permanent nickname, so both sides can refer to the same route even if things restart.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Delegation and state reporting expand the attack surface. The RFC RECOMMENDS using these extensions only over authenticated and encrypted sessions (TLS, per PCEPS) between a PCC and PCEs under the same administrative authority.

Three concerns are noted: LSP state snooping (exposing network topology/state to eavesdroppers), malicious PCE (flooding the PCC with updates), and malicious PCC (resource exhaustion at the PCE). Mitigations include limiting which PCEs receive state, revoking delegation at any time, and enforcing per-PCC resource limits signaled via PCNtf (Notification Type 4).
sections.plainLanguage: Sharing all route information is risky if someone listens in or if the helper turns bad. So the connection should be encrypted and authenticated, and the router can always cut off the helper.
